Over this period, the average annual premium for family coverage has surged +$5,884, or +26%.

To put this into perspective, CPI inflation has risen +13% over the same period, or half as much.

Since 1999, the average health insurance premium for a family has soared +$22,494, or +387%.

This represents an average annual growth rate of +6.1%, well above CPI inflation at +2.6% over the same period.

Health insurance has never been more expensive.

zh_summary: @steve_hanke: Trump spent last week trying to talk down oil and diesel markets, claiming more oil comes out of Hormuz than before the war, a line that even led the WSJ front page.
en_summary: @steve_hanke: Trump spent last week trying to talk down oil and diesel markets, claiming more oil comes out of Hormuz than before the war, a line that even led the WSJ front page.
text:
Last week started with Trump desperately attempting to talk down the markets for oil and refined products, such as diesel fuel. Among other things, Trump’s spin was that more oil is coming out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the war. This spin even made the lead story on the front page of The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday: “More Oil Is Now Coming Out of the Persian Gulf Than Before the Iran War.”

But there were many problems with that spin, including the fact that the price of Brent crude shot up by 7% after the Wall Street Journal’s lead story appeared. The narrative just didn’t make any sense. If there is so much oil coming out of the Strait, why does the price of Brent keep hitting new highs with each passing day? Two plus two does not equal five.

After the most recent price surge, Trump was forced to switch stories. On his social media platform, Truth Social, he threw in the towel on high prices and is now blaming them on Iran. But this narrative makes absolutely no sense either, since it was Trump’s war of choice against Iran that made the Strait functionally inoperative and caused the price of Brent to soar by 60% since the start of the war.

name: Kris Sidial🇺🇸
zh_summary: @Ksidiii: short interest charts miss the flows: most shops are not making outright short bets; banks providing balance sheet for speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure to ease margin requirements.
en_summary: @Ksidiii: short interest charts miss the flows: most shops are not making outright short bets; banks providing balance sheet for speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure to ease margin requirements.
text:
Everyone who keeps sharing these short interest charts is missing the flows behind them. Most shops are not taking outright short bets. This is another effort to ease margin requirements across the street: banks providing balance sheet for more speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure.

The sequence on the street looks like this:

HF manager: “I want more margin.”

Bank: “Things look risky in public AI bets, and we’re already lending a lot against private AI bets. For some clients, we’ll extend more financing, but only if they add more short exposure to improve their collateral scores.”

HF manager: “Okay, I’ll short more stock against my main bet.”

That is how you end up with short exposures that look astronomically high while many end users remain heavily long tech. The additional shorts are supporting the financing of their main bets.

Which also tells the bigger story on why raw equity financing rates haven’t blown out the way they did ahead of the big SpaceX IPO in June, despite the fact that lending is slowing.

And very large allocations from foundries online (they were doing these quals with Win Semi + 2 others back in 2023/2024), so they can actively monetize the bottleneck today. 

The other interesting reason why bottlenecks are important (aside from ASP hikes), is because qualifications convert much faster + more likely given incentives around supply scarcity.

-> This is while your biggest merchant laser companies making up the world's 600m+ EML/CW laser capacity like $COHR have redirected lasers to their own programs. $LITE sold out into 2029, Landmark also locked a lot of their capacity into 2027-2029. $AAOI was an expected player, but ended up redirecting lasers into their own transceiver programs too

zh_summary: Puru Saxena notes that drawdowns are normal for the S&P 500, with ~80-95% of time below prior peaks historically, and advises staying the course for long-term equity returns as volatility is the price of admission.
en_summary: Puru Saxena notes that drawdowns are normal for the S&P 500, with ~80-95% of time below prior peaks historically, and advises staying the course for long-term equity returns as volatility is the price of admission.
text:
Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

"I bought through all the cycles, and I have great relationships with the sellers, and they know I'm a closer. They know that my money is different than their money."

"All those guys are sidelined. They have redemption issues. They have pension funds saying, I want my money back. It's been 5 years, dude. I'm done."

"The institutions are all kind of trapped right now. And then there's this guy Grant Cardone that was going to retail investors and never went to their well."

"I have this money that was frowned upon that is now like, oh, your money's perfect. It's discretionary. It's really cheap money. I probably have access to the cheapest money in the world."

“Two years ago we had about 200 interns, and what we saw was those interns were really the first fully AI native. If you took AI away from them, I don't think they would be able to work.

So this past year, we decided we're going to hire a thousand interns. For a 5,000 person company. Over the course of the year.

It's just been amazing, because of the number of ideas that come from the interns. With AI, fewer people experiment faster, so having more ideas is great. And just seeing the way they use AI: they need to fill out a form, they reach for AI. And I still find myself, there are so many things where I'm like, 'Oh wait, I've just been doing this manually still.'”

The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries relative to puts is up to ~50 basis points, the highest since March 2025.

This marks a sharp reversal from a 250-basis-point premium for puts over calls in late September.

This suggests investors are increasingly betting on further gains in Treasury prices.

Furthermore, one options trade is targeting a drop in the 10Y Note Yield to ~4.60% within a month, involving ~65,000 contracts and costing ~$7 million in premium.

This comes as the 10Y Note Yield has declined below 5.00% for the first time since September 23rd, now down -40 basis points from the October 7th peak.

The bond market is seeing massive swings in price and sentiment.

text:
AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile are jointly lobbying the FCC to preserve existing rules as @SpaceX moves closer to launching its own independent cellular network that would compete directly with the three major U.S. carriers.

On Oct 20th, reps from all three major U.S. wireless carriers met with FCC officials to push back against proposed changes that would give satellite companies more freedom to offer cellular service.

The carriers urged the FCC to:
• Block satellite companies from using certain 5G frequencies currently used by wireless carriers.
• Keep rules requiring satellite companies to get permission from wireless carriers before using their licensed spectrum.
• Allow wireless carriers to maintain control over these agreements, including the ability to end them.
• Reconsider proposed interference limits to protect existing cellular networks.

Based on all the public communications from these carriers, and the lobbying, they are clearly worried that SpaceX's @Starlink Mobile network is going to be a major competitor to them. Starlink Mobile will become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum.

The FCC recently announced that they are considering new rules that could make it easier for satellite companies like SpaceX to offer cellular service without relying as heavily on existing wireless carriers, so this is partly what the three big carriers are fighting against.
